summary: Defines how an OSPF router advertises the types of Maximum SID Depth it supports, at node or link level. Controllers can use this to know whether a given stack of segment identifiers can be handled.

eli5.summary: A router says how many labels it can carry on a package, so planners do not pile on too many.

subtitle: How an OSPF router tells controllers how many segment labels it can push onto a packet.

tldr.problem: A controller that computes Segment Routing paths must not build a SID stack deeper than a node can impose, but it may have no other way to learn each node's limit.
tldr.mechanism: OSPF routers advertise Maximum SID Depth values per MSD-Type: a Node MSD TLV (type 12) in the Router Information Opaque LSA, and a Link MSD sub-TLV for individual links.
tldr.outcome: Controllers can learn node and link limits from the IGP itself. A link value overrides the node value, and the encoding can carry other MSD-Types later.

today: RFC 8476 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It defines the OSPF encoding; the MSD-Types registry is defined in RFC 8491.

sections.title: Why Routers Advertise MSD
sections.content:
When a centralized controller computes a Segment Routing (SR) path, it needs to know the Maximum SID Depth (MSD): how many Segment Identifiers (SIDs) a node or link can impose. Otherwise the computed SID stack could be deeper than the node can handle.

PCEP can signal MSD, but only if it is configured on the head-end. BGP-LS can export MSD, but it usually runs on only a few nodes. So the RFC says MSD capabilities SHOULD be advertised by every OSPF router in the network. The term OSPF here means both OSPFv2 and OSPFv3.

MSD can also be useful without SR: in a non-SR MPLS network it defines the maximum label depth.
sections.eli5: A planner builds routes for packets, but each router can only carry so many labels. Routers shout out their limit so the planner knows.

sections.title: Key Terms: MSD, SID and Imposition
sections.content:
MSD is the number of SIDs supported by a node or by a link on a node. A SID is defined in RFC 8402. Label imposition means modifying or adding labels to the outgoing label stack: replacing the top label, or pushing new ones. The number of labels imposed is the replaced labels plus the pushed ones.

The RFC expects further MSD-Types to be defined later, for example for entropy labels, for SIDs imposed through recirculation, or for SIDs tied to another data plane such as IPv6. This document only refers to the Signaling MSD type defined in RFC 8491.
sections.eli5: Imposition is how many stickers a router can put on a package. Different kinds of stickers may get their own limits later.

sections.title: The Node MSD TLV
sections.content:
The Node MSD TLV sits inside the OSPF Router Information (RI) Opaque LSA from RFC 7770. It carries the SID depth of the router that originated the LSA. Node MSD is the smallest MSD supported by the node on the interfaces configured for the advertising IGP instance. Values may be learned via a hardware API or provisioned.

The TLV is Type 12. Its Length is a multiple of 2 octets. The value is one or more pairs of a 1-octet MSD-Type and a 1-octet MSD-Value. MSD-Type comes from the IGP MSD-Types registry of RFC 8491. MSD-Value is 0 to 255; 0 means no ability to impose an MSD stack of any depth, and any other value MUST be the lowest value supported by any link configured for use by the OSPF instance.

The TLV is optional and applies to both OSPFv2 and OSPFv3.
sections.eli5: The router writes a note: type of limit, then the number. It can write several notes in one envelope.

sections.title: Handling Duplicate Node MSD TLVs
sections.content:
If a receiver sees several Node MSD TLVs from one router, it MUST use the first occurrence in the RI LSA. If the TLV appears in RI LSAs of different flooding scopes, the one in the area-scoped RI LSA MUST be used. If it appears in RI LSAs of the same scope, the one in the LSA with the numerically smallest Instance ID MUST be used and the others ignored.

The RI LSA can be flooded at link, area or AS scope. For Node MSD, area-scoped flooding is RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: If a router sends the same note twice, everyone follows the same rule about which copy counts, so they all agree.

sections.title: The Link MSD Sub-TLV
sections.content:
The Link MSD sub-TLV carries the MSD of the interface for a link. It has the same layout as the node TLV: pairs of MSD-Type and MSD-Value, with 0 meaning no ability to impose a stack of any depth. Any other value is that of the link when used as an outgoing interface.

In OSPFv2 it is an optional sub-TLV of the Extended Link TLV from RFC 7684, with type 6. In OSPFv3 it is an optional sub-TLV of the E-Router-LSA TLV from RFC 8362, with type 9.

If the same link carries this sub-TLV in several LSAs from the same router, receivers MUST use the one in the OSPFv2 Extended Link Opaque LSA with the smallest Opaque ID, or in the OSPFv3 E-Router-LSA with the smallest Link State ID. This situation SHOULD be logged as an error.
sections.eli5: A router can also write a limit for each road out of it, since different roads may carry different amounts.

sections.title: Combining Node and Link Values
sections.content:
When a Link MSD exists for an MSD-Type, it MUST take precedence over the Node MSD. If only the Node MSD is signaled, that value MUST be used for the link.

To keep flooding efficient, routers whose links all have the same MSD are RECOMMENDED to advertise just the Node MSD.

If neither a Node nor a Link MSD is advertised for a type, usually it only means the node does not support advertising that type. In some cases it might mean the function is not supported. The correct interpretation MUST be specified when an MSD-Type is defined, per RFC 8491.
sections.eli5: The rule for a specific road beats the rule for the whole router. If a router has the same limit everywhere, one note is enough.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: IANA allocated TLV type 12 (Node MSD) from the OSPF Router Information (RI) TLVs registry, sub-TLV type 6 (OSPFv2 Link MSD) from the OSPFv2 Extended Link TLV Sub-TLVs registry, and sub-TLV type 9 (OSPFv3 Link MSD) from the OSPFv3 Extended-LSA Sub-TLVs registry.
sections.eli5: The official number list now has entries for these notes, so everyone uses the same numbers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The usual OSPF security mechanisms apply, plus those of RFC 7770, RFC 7684 and RFC 8362. Implementations MUST detect malformed TLVs and sub-TLVs so attackers cannot crash the OSPF router or routing process. Such events SHOULD be counted or logged, and logging SHOULD be rate-limited to avoid a denial-of-service on the control plane.

A wrong MSD has consequences. A value that is too small may make path computation fail to find a viable path. A value that is too large may lead to an attempt to build a path the head-end cannot support. The information could also tell an attacker how to cause this. The RFC states there is no DoS risk specific to this extension and that it is not vulnerable to replay attacks.
sections.eli5: A wrong number could make the planner fail or ask for too much. Routers must also not break when they get a garbled note.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Multiple of 2 octets; total length of the value field.

fields.name: MSD-Type
fields.desc: Kind of MSD, from the IGP MSD-Types registry.

fields.name: MSD-Value
fields.desc: 0 to 255; 0 means no ability to impose a stack.
